DILG BAGONG P'L'P'NAS Republic of the Philippines DEPARTMENT OF THE INTERIOR AND LOCAL GOVERNMENT DILG-NAPOLCOM Center, EDSA cor. Quezon Avenue, West Triangle, Quezon City www.dilg.gov.ph OILG OPINION NO. AUG 21 2024 ATTY. MARY JUSTICE P. AURELIO-YAP Provincial Legal Officer Provincial Capitol Compound, Brgy. Cabidianan, Nabunturan, Davao de Oro Province Dear Atty. Aurelio-Yap: This has reference to the letter dated xxx requesting for an opinion concerning the municipal ordinances of the Municipality of Montevista and Pantukan. The facts and circumstances are as follows: The Municipality of Montevista enacted Municipal Ordinances No. 276 increasing the tax rates from the previously enacted Municipal Tax Ordinance. It is the contention that the basis for the 10% increase are the rates prescribed in the previously enacted tax code of the municipality. On the other hand, the Municipality of Pantukan enacted Municipal Ordinance No. 167 s. 2023 re: "An Ordinance Providing Regulation and Mechanism in Phasing Out the Use of Single-Use Plastic and Polystyrene Products in the Municipality of Pantukan, Province of Davao de Oro and Imposing Penalties for Violation Thereof'. In said ordinance, sixty percent (60%) of the collected fines from the violators shall be given to the LGU for Solid Waste Management Activities while the remaining forty percent (40%) shall be given to person/s or associations who report any violation of the ordinance. The ordinance seeks to incentivize those person/s who intend to report any violation for the use of single-use plastic and polystyrene products. The following points of clarification were raised, to wit: (I) What serves as the basis for adjusting tax rates in the municipality: the tax ordinance previously enacted five (5) years ago or the rates specified in the Local Government Code? (2) Can the Sangguniang Bayan validly pass an ordinance providing for a Collection Scheme that allocates fines and penalties collected from the ordinance violations, with sixty percent (60%) allocated to Solid Waste Management activities and forty percent (40%) designed for individuals or associations who report violations of the ordinance to authorized enforcing agency/office? Anent the first query, it is this level's opinion that the basis for adjusting tax rates is the adjusted or prevailing tax rate. "Matino, Mahusay at Maasahan" Trunkline No.: 8876-34-54

The Supreme Court in National Power Corporation vs. City of Cabanatuanl, the Local Government Code of 1991 (LGC), in granting powers upon LGUs the power to tax, does not dictate the tax rate to be imposed by the LGUs but merely sets the minimum or the maximum, leaving upon the respective sanggunian the determination of the actual rates to be imposed in accordance with their needs and capabilities. Under Sec. 1912 of the LGC, local government units have the authority to adjust the rates of a tax ordinance once every five (5) years, but not to exceed ten percent (10%) of the rates fixed under therein. This provision was discussed by the Supreme Court in Hon. Leila M. de Lima vs. City of Manila3, to wit: " xxx The option to increase the tax rates under the LGC arises every five (5) years reckoned from the enactment of the ordinance sought to be adjusted. The decision of whether or not to exercise such option falls upon the LGU, through their respective sanggunian taking into consideration the status of each industry balanced with the needs of their respective territory. In the event that the LGU fails to make such adjustment within the five (5)-year period, the option to increase the prevailing ordinance remains open until such right is exercised, at which point, the five (5)-year period of limitation starts to run again. On the other hand, were the LGU decides to make such adjustment, the basis for the increase would be the prevailing tax rate. Foreseeing that the compounding of interest would invite fear that its eventual accumulation would become unduly burdensome, the taxpayers should be reassured of the built-in measures under the LGC to restrict the power of the LGUs in this regard." In Mindanao Shopping Destination Corporation, et. al vs. Hon. Rodrigo R. Duterte, et.a14, " xxx Thus, dictated by justice and fairness, in its initial attempt to implement the LGC, Davao City should, at the very least, start with 1 % (the minimum tax rate) as provided under Section 143 (d) of the LGC. Considering that 1 1 years had already elapsed from its implementing in 2006, Davao City could adjust its tax rate twice now which will make its adjusted tax rate for retailers pegged at 1.2%, in accordance with Section 191 of the LGC. To clarify, from 2006-2011 (first 5 years), the initial tax rate should start with 1 %; from 2011-2016 (next 5 years) - 1.1%, thus, for the years 2017-2021, the tax adjustment is 1.21%. However, for this purpose, Davao City should pass an ordinance to give effect to the above-discussed tax adjustments." Based on the foregoing, the tax adjustments must be based on the adjusted or prevailing tax rate. However, to find Section 191 applicable, the Supreme Court in Mindanao Shopping Destination, et.al vs. Hon. Rodrigo R. Duterte. et.al ruled that the application of Section 191 requires the concurrence of two elements (1) there is a tax ordinance that already imposes tax in accordance with the provisions of the LGC; and (2) there is a second tax ordinance that made adjustment on the tax rate fixed by the first tax ordinance. GR No. 149110, April 9, 2003. Section 191. Authority of Local Govemment Units to Adjust Rates of Tax Ordinances. - Local government units shall have the authority to adjust the tax rates as prescribed herein not oftener than once every five (5) years, but in no case shall such adjustment exceed ten percent (10%) of the rates fixed under this Code. G.R. NO. 222886, October 17, 2018. G.R. NO. 211093, June 6, 2017. Page 2 of 3

Thus, in order for Sec. 191 to be applicable, it is imperative that both tax ordinances were enacted during the effectivity of the LGC. Anent the second query, this level opines that the collection has some legal infirmities. The fees imposed in Municipal Ordinance 167 s. 2023 is deemed to be regulatory in nature as it seeks to regulate the use of single-use plastic and polystyrene products in the Municipality of Pantukan. Being regulatory in nature, the imposition must also bear a reasonable relation to the probable expenses of regulation, taking into account not only the costs of direct regulation but also its incidental consequences as we115. If the regulatory fee produces revenue in excess of the cost of the regulation, inspection and licensing, it will be considered excessive6. This level posits that the collection of penalties being exacted must only be commensurate to the costs in which the municipality may suffer in the implementation of its ordinance. To exact fees to incentivize person/s or associations who report these violations would mean that the penalties being collected is excessive as it does not pertain to the costs of regulation. Furthermore, the ordinance failed to provide proper mechanisms or guidelines in providing transparency and avoidance of potential conflict of interests in order to accurately provide such incentives to possible reporters of violators. This opinion shall be without prejudice to any contrary opinion rendered by more competent authorities and/or the courts. We hope to have assisted you on this matter. Thank you very much. Very truly yours, Y A THORITY OF THE SECRETARY: JU VICTOR R. LLAMAS ersecretary for External, Legal and Legislative Affairs USELLNJVRULLLS-LRALLD,'Sbl s Progressive Development Corporation vs. Quezon City, GR No. L-36081, April 2, 1989. 6 Municipality of san Mateo vs. Smart Communications lnc, GR NO. 219506, June 23, 2021.
